documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effect of utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) in social commerce on increasing consumer engagement, specifically in terms of engagement and conversion rates. It also examines the role of flow experience in strengthening this relationship. Design/methodology/approach This study collected data from 354 Indonesian social commerce shoppers. Covariance based Structural Equation Modeling was employed to analyze the data following the two-stage procedure. First, the measurement model was assessed for validity and reliability. Second, the structural hypothesis model was evaluated to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings The utilization of AI significantly influences social commerce visitor interactions in terms of engagement and conversion. Both variables can enhance customer satisfaction, thereby impacting repurchase intention. Flow experience also strengthens the relationship between engagement and satisfaction, offering practical guidance for creating immersive and enjoyable user experiences. Originality/value This study extends the existing social commerce and AI literature by positioning flow experience as a moderator, explaining how and when engagement and conversion translate into satisfaction. Unlike previous models that primarily focus on direct effects, this research introduces psychological mechanisms that capture the conditional and experiential nature of AI-driven interactions, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of consumer behavior in social commerce.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Petrol station attendants (PSAs) are chronically exposed to benzene, toluene, and xylene (BTX) — hazardous volatile organic compounds present in commercial petrol — through daily fuel dispensing, yet occupational BTX monitoring data, particularly from Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), remain critically limited. Comprehensive exposure assessment of BTX in occupational settings spans four complementary monitoring approaches, organised here using the Environmental Public Health Paradigm (EPHP) as a conceptual lens: environmental monitoring, personal monitoring, biological monitoring, and biological-effect monitoring. The extent to which published studies have simultaneously applied all four monitoring domains among PSAs remains unknown. Methods A literature search was performed in PubMed, Medline, and Google Scholar for original articles published from January 1992 to December 2024. This narrative review considered studies reporting data on at least one of the four monitoring domains among PSAs or comparable petrol sector workers. Results Environmental and personal monitoring document elevated BTX concentrations at refuelling sites — frequently exceeding international occupational exposure limits (OELs) in LMIC settings — with benzene concentrations ranging from 0.1 to over 6 ppm across reviewed studies. Biological monitoring confirms systemic benzene absorption, with urinary S-phenylmercapturic acid (SPMA) and urinary benzene (U-BEN) emerging as the most sensitive and specific biomarkers. Biological-effect monitoring documents consistent genotoxicity, haematotoxicity, oxidative stress, and immunological disruption in PSA populations globally. To our knowledge, no published study identified in this review has simultaneously implemented all four monitoring domains in a single PSA cohort. Conclusion BTX exposure among PSAs constitutes a significant and underaddressed occupational health problem, with a disproportionate burden in LMICs. The absence of integrated multi-domain monitoring evidence limits the development of evidence-based occupational health policy for this vulnerable workforce. Future studies combining all four monitoring domains in a single, well-characterised cohort are recommended.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background County hospitals and township health centers in China provide frontline care for time-sensitive neurological emergencies, and three-year junior-college clinical medicine programs are an important pathway into this workforce. We evaluated a faculty-supervised artificial intelligence (AI)-supported BOPPPS (Bridge-in, Objectives, Pre-assessment, Participatory Learning, Post-assessment, and Summary) and case-based learning (CBL) instructional package among junior-college medical interns. Methods In this prospective, batch-stratified randomized educational study, 118 interns from 12 monthly rotation batches were assigned to AI-supported BOPPPS-CBL ( n = 58) or conventional BOPPPS-CBL ( n = 60) during a one-month neurology rotation. The intervention used standardized DeepSeek prompts for Socratic questioning, error-focused feedback, and structured reflection under faculty supervision. The primary endpoint was the total score on a locally developed four-station simulated neurological-emergency assessment (0–100). Secondary outcomes included a written examination, while learner-reported questionnaire items were exploratory. Regression models adjusted for rotation batch, baseline academic performance, and digital literacy. The study was not prospectively registered; no public trial registration identifier or registry URL exists, and no publicly time-stamped protocol or statistical analysis plan was available. Results All 118 participants completed the primary assessment. Mean total scores were 82.07 in the AI-supported group and 76.43 in the control group, with an adjusted between-group difference of 5.67 points (95% CI, 2.86–8.49; P < 0.001; adjusted Cohen's d = 0.74). In secondary station-specific analyses, only lesion localization met the multiplicity-adjusted threshold (adjusted mean difference, 2.58 points; 95% CI, 1.25–3.91; P < 0.001; adjusted d = 0.71). A Station 2-specific ICC was not estimated. Post hoc sensitivity analyses excluding the station containing reused case contexts yielded standardized estimates of similar magnitude but could not exclude cueing or carry-over. Written-examination estimates were smaller and imprecise. Exploratory learner-reported findings indicated greater perceived preparation-time burden in the AI-supported group. Conclusion Assignment to the faculty-supervised AI-supported BOPPPS-CBL package was associated with higher scores on a locally developed simulated neurological-emergency assessment than conventional BOPPPS-CBL. These findings do not establish transfer to workplace clinical performance or patient outcomes. Multicenter studies using independent assessment cases, longer-term follow-up, and workplace-based outcomes are warranted.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Human-AI collaboration is increasingly relevant in consequential areas where AI recommendations support human discretion. However, human-AI teams’ effectiveness, capability, and fairness highly depend on human perceptions of AI. Positive fairness perceptions have been shown to foster trust and acceptance of AI recommendations. Yet, work on confirmation bias highlights that humans selectively adhere to AI recommendations that align with their expectations and beliefs—despite those recommendations not being necessarily correct or fair. This raises the question of whether confirmation bias also transfers to the alignment of gender bias between human and AI decisions. In our study, we examine how gender bias alignment and the presence of explanations accompanying the AI recommendation influence fairness perceptions, human self-confidence, and reliance on the AI system. Findings from two 2 \(\times\) 2 between-subjects studies underscore the relationship between gender-bias alignment, fairness perceptions, and reliance, demonstrating that merely constructing a “formally fair” AI system is insufficient for optimal human–AI collaboration. Ultimately, AI recommendations are likely to be overridden when the system's biases do not align with those of its users.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the nature of work and creating growing concerns about future employment among university students. Fear of AI replacement may influence students’ psychological well-being and perceptions of career security. The present study examined the relationship between fear of AI replacement, anxiety, career insecurity, and life satisfaction among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional correlational design was used with a sample of 400 university students aged 18–25 years, comprising 200 males and 200 females. Participants completed measures of fear of AI replacement, career insecurity, anxiety, and life satisfaction. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis. The findings indicated that fear of AI replacement was positively associated with anxiety (β = .43, p < .001) and career insecurity (β = .52, p < .001), while it was negatively associated with life satisfaction (β = −.31, p < .001). Regression analyses showed that fear of AI replacement explained 18% of the variance in anxiety, 27% in career insecurity, and 10% in life satisfaction. The findings suggest that greater fear of AI replacement may be associated with increased anxiety and career insecurity and reduced life satisfaction among university students. Universities should consider integrating AI literacy, career counselling, employability skills, and psychological support to help students adapt to AI-related changes in the future market.

Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing clients’ raw data, but parameter exchange can impose substantial communication costs and usually requires compatible model architectures. Federated distillation (FD) instead transfers predictive or intermediate knowledge through knowledge distillation (KD), which can support heterogeneous models and reduce communication in suitable settings. These benefits are not automatic: their magnitude depends on the transmitted knowledge, reference data, communication schedule, and threat model. This survey provides a challenge-centered synthesis of FD. We first formalize a representative public-data, response-based FD protocol and then organize existing methods by the FL challenges they address, including data, system, and model heterogeneity, client drift, catastrophic forgetting, communication cost, and privacy risk. We further review applications in industrial engineering, computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, including recent federated adaptation of large language models. Finally, we identify five research priorities: richer transferred knowledge, joint treatment of interacting forms of heterogeneity, communication-aware distillation, threat-model-driven privacy protection, and standardized theory, benchmarks, and evaluation.

Federated learning enables distributed training without exchanging original images, but non-IID data and class imbalance can degrade model performance. In this study, FedMobileNet is presented as a decentralized machine learning system based on MobileNetV2 for multiclass classification. The training instances were spread among four simulated clients using a Dirichlet-based non-IID partitioning method (with α = 1.0) so that each client had at least five samples per class. The model used a multiclass focal loss with class weights set to α = [2.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0] and γ = 2.0; minority oversampling was not applied. The model that achieved the highest validation AUC at the checkpoint was selected and then evaluated once on the separate test dataset. In the test evaluation described here, FedMobileNet reached an accuracy of 89.4% and a macro-AUC of 0.97; the class-wise F1-scores were 0.81 for adenocarcinoma, 0.77 for large cell carcinoma, 0.97 for normal tissue, and 0.83 for squamous cell carcinoma. These results correspond directly to findings from a specific simulated federated configuration. They should not be interpreted as proof of clinical effectiveness or as evidence that the method is ready for deployment. The study uses a single public CT dataset, a single fixed random seed, and a specific client partition. It did not include analysis with repeated seeds and different partitions, external clinical validation, or direct measurements of memory, energy, communication cost, and inference latency. For this reason, the framework is described as resource-conscious rather than having been experimentally validated as resource-efficient for clinical or edge deployment.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to develop an interpretable, two-stage artificial intelligence (AI) system (fundus fluorescein angiography [FFA]-SegGPT) designed to optimize the clinical workflow of diabetic retinopathy (DR) FFA interpretation and reduce the risk of factual inaccuracies common in end-to-end models. Methods: We developed a cross-modal system that decouples lesion quantification from report generation. A segmentation module first explicitly segments non-perfusion areas (NPAs) and neovascularization (NV). These segmentation maps then serve as visual constraints to guide an evidence-based report generator, ensuring diagnostic text is strictly grounded in detected lesions. Results: In a simulated clinical workflow, AI-aided reporting significantly reduced mean interpretation time by 50% (from 8.13 ± 0.47 to 4.09 ± 0.21 minutes, P < 0.001) and improved median report quality (4.0 vs. 3.5, P < 0.001) compared to manual interpretation. Objectively, the model achieved high Dice Similarity Coefficients (NV = 85.35% and NPAs = 86.49%) and maintained high semantic fidelity for report generation (BERTScore = 0.91), with robust generalization demonstrated across three external cohorts. Conclusions: FFA-SegGPT enhances both the efficiency and quality of DR diagnostics. By decoupling lesion quantification from report generation, the system provides a transparent, dual-output mechanism that reduces the risk of factual inaccuracies, offering an interpretable workflow to facilitate safe clinical adoption. Translational Relevance: This interpretable AI system optimizes the clinical workflow of DR by providing verifiable lesion segmentation and automated reporting, potentially reducing clinician workload and standardizing diagnostic quality.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Financial sustainability remains a persistent challenge for non-governmental organizations (NGOs), which frequently depend on government grants and donor funding. In the absence of stable and diversified income streams, NGOs struggle with strategic planning, staff retention, and consistent service delivery. This systematic review synthesizes current scholarship on financial sustainability in the non-profit sector, focusing on key obstacles and the strategies used to address them. Utilizing the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework and NVivo 12, peer-reviewed studies were systematically identified, screened, and analyzed. The findings indicate that the most significant barriers are related to financial and resource constraints, organizational capability gaps, and external contextual challenges. Key strategies to overcome these barriers include revenue diversification, partnership and resource mobilization, financial resource management, and technology use. In addition to revenue diversification, the thematic analysis highlights the importance of partnerships and resource mobilization, financial resource management, and integrating artificial intelligence as complementary strategies. The analysis also identifies four organizational enablers of financial sustainability: organizational capacity, leadership and governance, stakeholder trust, and volunteer capacity. These results emphasize the need for context-specific, multidimensional approaches to strengthen NGOs' financial resilience and ensure the long-term sustainability of their programs. By consolidating insights from diverse studies, this review provides a comprehensive overview of financial sustainability research in the nonprofit sector, identifies critical gaps for further investigation, and offers practical guidance for practitioners and policymakers.

First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Iván Hidalgo-Cenalmor is first author on ‘ NucleiSky enables cross-scale multimodal registration of microscopy data using nuclei constellations’, published in JCS. Iván is a PhD student in the lab of Guillaume Jacquemet at the Turku Bioscience Centre, Turku, Finland, where his work focuses on developing computational and image analysis tools for biological imaging, including microscopy image registration and explainable artificial intelligence.

A bstract Defect conformal field theories have special operators of protected dimension known as displacements and tilts. They arise due to the breaking of global symmetries by the defect and the normalisations of their two-point functions are characteristics of the defect. In the case of surface defects, these normalisations are related to some of the anomaly coefficients in the surface effective action. To study these operators and their flows between different defect renormalization group fixed points we present an elegant approach using conformal perturbation theory that easily reproduces the known examples from the critical Wilson-Fisher O( N ) model in 4 − ε dimensions and allows us to construct new ones in other multiscalar theories. In all the systems that we study the flows are short and under full control, as is the change of the displacement and tilt normalizations. We point out some novel features like the existence of vortices when the defect conformal manifold is not simply connected. In addition to regular human labour, this work relied heavily on generative AI; see full disclosure in methodology section.

Abstract Objectives Cross-border care, teleradiology, and international referral pathways increasingly require radiology report translation, but isolated mistranslations may alter clinical meaning. We evaluated German-to-English machine translation of radiology reports and correction-based localization of text requiring review. Materials and methods In this retrospective study, 310 de-identified German radiology reports from June and July 2025 were translated into English with DeepL. Eight radiologists assigned 5-point quality scores and corrected perceived errors. Thirty reports were reviewed by all eight readers, and 280 reports were assigned for single-reader evaluation, yielding 520 evaluations. Automated metrics and large language model judges were tested for report-level identification of translations requiring review; a correction-based segment-level edit-prediction model was evaluated on held-out shared reports. Results Most translations were rated good or excellent (339/520, 65.2%), but clinically important mistranslations involved diagnosis, anatomy, and radiologic terminology. Agreement was low for ordinal quality scores (Krippendorff α = 0.078, p = 0.006) but high for expert corrections (pairwise “bilingual evaluation understudy”–BLEU = 83.0, p < 0.001). In the conservative primary screen of 30 shared reports, no automated method discriminated translations requiring review (area under receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] = 0.51–0.65; p = 0.100–0.920). The final edit-prediction model achieved a concordance index of 0.697 and an AUC of 0.731 for segments edited by at least six of eight readers. Conclusion Machine-translated radiology reports were often acceptable on average, but translations containing errors requiring expert review persisted. Expert corrections were more reproducible than ordinal quality scores and supported localization of text requiring human review. Key Points Question Cross-border radiology workflows increasingly require report translation, but fluent machine translations may still contain meaning-changing errors requiring expert review for safe care. Findings Most machine translations were rated good or excellent, yet clinically important mistranslations occurred, and automated report-level metrics did not reliably identify reports needing review. Relevance statement Machine translation may support cross-border radiology workflows, but clinically important mistranslations in otherwise fluent reports require human-in-the-loop oversight and tools that localize text requiring expert review.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study aims to compare human and artificial intelligence (AI) responses to Indonesian and English folklore. The Indonesian folklore is represented by Bawang Merah and Bawang Putih as well as Timun Mas, while the English folklore is represented by Cinderella and Jack and the Beanstalk. Employing a descriptive qualitative approach, this research examines reader responses through intellectual, emotional, and cultural dimensions. The study applies the synchronic reception theory, which involves analyzing responses from contemporary human readers in comparison with those generated by AI. The findings reveal a convergence in intellectual responses, where both human readers and AI predominantly exhibit positive interpretations of the four stories. In contrast, emotional responses demonstrate significant variation. Readers show diverse reactions, unlike the more uniform responses generated by AI. These differences are shaped by familiarity with the narratives, as well as cultural, moral, religious, and individual values while AI maintained a consistently positive tone emphasizing narrative coherence without cultural bias. These findings contribute valuable insights to the fields of literary reception studies, cross-entity interpretation, and the implications of technology-assisted literary engagement.

topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Achieving accurate signature verification is critical in many contexts including financial transactions and legal contracts, for reasons of security and fraud risk. The authors describe an offline signature verification system called ForgeXplain that uses hand engineered image features in conjunction with machine learning algorithms and explainable AI. From pre-processed signature images the system extracts 23 hand designed geometric and intensity features that in turn feed into support vector machine (SVM) and random forest (RF) models in order to predict fake from real signatures, with SHAP values explaining the decision on a feature-by-feature basis. A test of 1,320 real and 1,320 fake signatures from CEDAR offline found that Random Forest was correct 91.5 percent of the time and achieved a ROC-AUC score of 0.966, better than SVM. This shows that ForgeXplain can tackle off-line signature forgery detection effectively and faithfully.

Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

Comparative research on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and artificial intelligence usually treats national institutions and firm leadership separately. Institutional studies ask which countries make adoption easier. Leadership studies ask which managers make adoption happen. In founder-led SMEs, where one person often holds most decision rights, these questions cannot be separated. This study argues that the same founder can be more or less effective at leading generative AI adoption depending on the institutional setting, and that the direction of this effect depends on the type of readiness the founder has. We develop the Founder-Institution Fit (FIF) model. It builds on the Founder Readiness Framework (FRF-4) proposed by Sarkisyan (2026) and combines two founder composites, structural and psychological readiness, with three national parameters: the depth of the market for external expertise, the strength of internal delegation norms, and regulatory clarity. We apply the model to four stylized founder archetypes in Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Both are high-income economies, but they differ sharply in institutional type. The illustrative analysis gives three findings. First, psychological readiness works as a multiplier. A founder who is low on it achieves little in either country, whatever institutional support is available. Second, the country advantage reverses with the founder's profile. Founders whose readiness rests mainly on learning orientation gain more in the British setting, which offers a deep market for outside expertise. Founders whose readiness rests mainly on identity plasticity gain more in the Swiss setting, which supports internal delegation. Third, once regulatory differences are neutralized, the crossover follows a closed-form threshold: the British setting is preferred when the ratio of learning orientation to identity plasticity exceeds 4:3. We discuss implications for founders, boards, advisors, and policymakers and set out an agenda for empirical calibration.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being considered across pharmaceutical manufacturing, quality management, maintenance, supply chain, regulatory activities and product development. However, the central challenge for pharmaceutical organizations is no longer whether AI can generate technical possibilities, but how AI can be converted into reliable, measurable and compliant operational value. This conceptual paper develops an AI-to-Value framework for pharmaceutical operations by integrating five dimensions: use-case relevance, data readiness, model credibility, GMP and governance controls, and human decision accountability. The framework proposes that AI value creation is mediated by data quality and organizational readiness and moderated by risk-based governance and human oversight. Illustrative use cases are discussed across tablet manufacturing, visual inspection, predictive maintenance, supply planning, deviation management and workforce development. The paper further proposes research propositions that can be empirically tested using case studies, surveys or quantitative modelling. The contribution is a practical conceptual architecture that connects AI adoption with operational excellence, rather than treating AI implementation as a technology acquisition exercise. The framework suggests that successful pharmaceutical AI requires a progression from isolated pilots to governed, measurable and scalable intelligent operations.

documents.abstract: This study aims to explore the technological sovereignty of urban Indian university students with respect to the use of AI towards Viksit Bharat 2047. It demonstrates the current state of AI usage orientation among the younger generation as AI consumers or AI value creators and strives to assess the path that we are journeying in towards a developed nation. With the current digital era, AI tools seek to help in research, improve problem-solving skills, and encourage innovative thinking. Generative AI and prompt templates help in comprehending the cognitive abilities of university students using digital learning platforms and enable the students to utilize artificial intelligence to design creative solutions and have an entrepreneurial mindset. Ultimately, this research delves into the future scope regarding urban Indian university students' readiness in terms of automotive technology towards Viksit Bharat 2047.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being used within higher education to enhance curriculum design, automate academic tasks, and personalise learning. Despite this, little is known about teaching academics’ attitudes, intentions and behaviours and in turn, how they use and plan to use GenAI in practice. This qualitative study explored teaching academic staff attitudes, intentions and behaviours regarding their use and future use of GenAI. Data was collected via five open ended questions focusing on current teaching practices. The Theory of Planned Behaviour informed the analytical process. Academic staff were drawn from 20 different disciplines across 24 countries. Six main themes were identified: Efficiency and Automation, Ethics and Authenticity, Quality, Customised Learning, Institutional Policy-Practice and Sociocultural Implications. Overall, there was a dichotomy in responses. Participants noted that while GenAI could streamline teaching and enhance resource quality, it might also increase short-term workload and reduce the role of human judgement, risking unreliable outputs. They also highlighted limited institutional policies, strategies, and training. These attitudes have implications for updating policies, practical strategies, and meaningful training in higher education institutions.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study examined the effects of an educational intervention on senior high school Greek students’ perceptions of climate change, motivation for active citizenship and volunteering, and sense of individual and collective responsibility in crisis management. A repeated-measures design was employed, with participants (N = 29 before; N = 25 after) completing validated self-report scales before and after the intervention. Results indicated a modest overall improvement in mean scores across all variables following the intervention. Significant correlations among the three domains were observed both pre- and post-intervention, but with stronger associations after the intervention. Cluster analysis revealed three participant response profiles indicating heterogeneous intervention effects. The findings highlight the nuanced nature of students’ cognitive engagement with climate change and civic responsibility, underscoring the potential of targeted educational interventions to foster sustainable, pro-social attitudes.

Artificial intelligence perfectly transforming the sphere of education and offering adaptive architecture of learning, automatizing evaluation processes, and increasing activities of learners, is here to stay. This chapter provides a systematic analysis of the best approaches to establish AI in environments of classroom settings, which include adaptive learning environments, virtual tutors, generative AI applications, intelligent recommender systems, and automated assessment systems. Based on empirical research and feasible case examples, the chapter outlines how AI can reduce the administrative load, is capable of recognizing instructional gaps, and manages different needs of student groups. It also questions the relevant ethical issues, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the necessity of being a life-long learner, which defines the classical significance of professional development in teachers who are already walking on this changing ground.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) is a fundamental approach for increasing oil production from mature reservoirs, in which a significant fraction of the oil remains trapped due to capillary forces, unfavorable mobility ratios, heterogeneity, and preferential flow. This review analyzes the evolution of physics applied to EOR between 2000 and 2026, highlighting the transition from methods based on the optimization of isolated properties toward integrated, multiscale, and reservoir-specific strategies. The main mechanisms associated with low-salinity water and smart water, polymers, surfactants, ASP processes, miscible CO₂ and CO₂-foam, nanotechnology, microfluidics, and digital rock physics are discussed. The analysis demonstrates that mobility, capillarity, wettability, interfacial tension, miscibility, rheology, and transport act in a coupled manner, making it inadequate to evaluate any technology based on a single performance parameter. The development of microfluidics, computed tomography, and digital rock reconstructions has expanded the ability to directly observe pore-scale phenomena and relate them to macroscopic responses. More recently, physics-informed machine learning, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), neural networks, and neural operators have been used to integrate experimental data and physical laws for the prediction and optimization of recovery processes. Parallelly, it is demonstrated that the evolution of contemporary EOR extends beyond production maximization by directly aligning with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the 2030 Agenda, highlighting resource optimization in mature fields (SDG 12 - Responsible Consumption and Production), digitalization and AI innovation (SDG 9 - Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), permanent geological carbon storage via CCUS (SDG 13 - Climate Action), and transitional energy efficiency (SDG 7 - Affordable and Clean Energy). It is concluded that the main frontier of contemporary EOR does not lie in the search for a universal technology, but rather in the combination of physical mechanisms, experimental characterization, computational modeling, artificial intelligence, and global sustainability guidelines. This integration establishes the foundations for intelligent, adaptive, multiscale, sustainable EOR guided by the characteristics and uncertainties of each reservoir. It is concluded that the main frontier of contemporary EOR does not lie in the search for a universal technology, but rather in the combination of physical mechanisms, experimental characterization, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence. This integration establishes the foundations for intelligent, adaptive, multiscale EOR guided by the characteristics and uncertainties of each reservoir.

Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons. We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round. Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them. WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments. Weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation. Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction. Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.

The use of large language models (LLMs) in finance has expanded rapidly, yet general-purpose systems face recurring problems in high-risk and regulated applications: Unsupported factual generation, weak reasoning across text, tables, charts, and numerical data, and limited traceability of model-assisted decisions. This study conducts a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta Analyses (PRISMA)-informed structured review of 67 studies, principally published between January 2020 and March 2026, with three foundational pre-2020 studies retained through backward citation tracking. It develops a qualitative analytical and diagnostic framework with three pathways: Specialized knowledge modeling, task-constrained multimodal reasoning, and Trust-by-Design. A study-level evidence map and an explicit coding protocol show how the pathways were derived. The framework is used to compare BloombergGPT, FinGPT, FinTral, Fin-o1, Fin-R1, and Agentar-Fin-R1 through common criteria for knowledge controls, modality handling, lifecycle governance, evidence quality, and deployment maturity. The case analysis distinguishes model-paper design descriptions, developer reported benchmark results, platform-level deployment reports, and prospective applications. The analysis indicates that financial LLMs differ materially in how they organize domain knowledge, coordinate heterogeneous inputs, and govern model use across the lifecycle. Agentar-Fin-R1 illustrates the framework; the case does not validate the framework or establish independently observed production performance. The paper provides a structured basis for assessing domain-specific financial LLMs and connects responsible model design with sustainable financial innovation through durable governance arrangements, controlled model and compliance risk, responsible scaling, financial inclusion, and institutional resilience. Received: 1 April 2026 | Revised: 2 September 2026 | Accepted: 20 September 2026 Conflicts of Interest The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement Tables S1–S4 in the Supplementary Materials provide the prospective replication protocol, the study-level evidence map for the 67-study corpus, the code-to-pathway derivation and threshold rationale, and the register of seven sources outside the review corpus. The original query-level exports, source-specific yields, and coder-level screening logs were not retained. Data sharing is not applicable to this article as no new data were created or analyzed in this study. documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence marks a shift from static prediction toward systems that perceive, reason, act, verify, and adapt through closed-loop interaction with external environments. Although large multimodal models provide the representational substrate for this shift, practical agency emerges only when model inference is embedded within memory, planning, tool use, environment interfaces, verification, and oversight mechanisms. We formalize the notion of an agentic AI system, distinguish it from single-turn assistants, scripted workflows, retrieval-augmented generation, and classical embodied controllers, and propose a taxonomy covering model substrates, observation spaces, memory, planning, action interfaces, multi-agent coordination, evaluation, and autonomy constraints. We then synthesize learning and optimization paradigms for agents, including supervised trajectory tuning, tool-use adaptation, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, process rewards, verifier-guided search, test-time scaling, memory-driven adaptation, and distillation. Across domains such as web search, software engineering, multimodal reasoning, embodied control, scientific discovery, and enterprise automation, we analyze the factors shaping agent performance and reliability. We further examine benchmarks, evaluation protocols, safety considerations, governance challenges, and open research problems in long-horizon reasoning, memory management, multimodal grounding, and trustworthy deployment. A companion repository tracking developments in agentic AI is available at https://github.com/Tajamul21/awesome-agentic-ai.

Purpose Drawing upon work–family boundary theory and the significance of employees career sustainability amid widespread artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, this study examines the impact of AI awareness on two indicators of career sustainability (i.e. well-being and productivity) via work–family conflict and the moderating role of work–family segmentation preference in this relationship. Design/methodology/approach We collected data from 421 subordinate-supervisor dyads across multiple industries using a two-wave design and tested the hypotheses with structural equation modeling in Mplus. Findings The results indicated a negative effect of AI awareness on career sustainability (i.e. subordinate-rated well-being and supervisor-rated productivity) via work–family conflict. Additionally, work–family segmentation preference functions as an important boundary condition, weakening the positive relationship between AI awareness and work–family conflict and attenuating the indirect negative effect of AI awareness on both well-being and productivity. Research limitations/implications This study offers three key theoretical contributions. First, it identifies AI awareness as a novel antecedent of career sustainability, extending research within socio-technical organizational contexts. Second, drawing on work–family boundary theory, it reveals a cross-domain spillover mechanism through which AI awareness undermines career sustainability via work–family conflict. Finally, it highlights work–family segmentation preference as a boundary management strategy that buffers the negative effects of AI awareness, enriching understanding of individual-level moderators in AI-related career research. Practical implications This study offers several practical implications. First, organizations should mitigate the negative impact of AI awareness on career sustainability by fostering balanced human–AI collaboration through clear job design, AI literacy training, and supportive feedback systems. Second, promoting work–family boundary management – such as, encouraging segmentation preferences and family-supportive policies – can reduce work–family conflict and enhance employee well-being. Finally, integrating boundary management skills into recruitment and development practices helps organizations sustain both employee happiness and productivity in AI-driven workplaces. Social implications As AI becomes increasingly embedded in workplaces, its influence extends beyond productivity to employees' family life and long-term career sustainability. This study suggests that unmanaged AI-related stress may erode well-being and work effectiveness through work–family conflict. The findings highlight the broader social need to promote healthier human–AI collaboration, clearer work–life boundaries, and more sustainable career development. By encouraging AI literacy, boundary management, and supportive organizational norms, organizations can help reduce the unintended social costs of technological disruption and foster employee well-being, family harmony, and sustainable employment in the AI era. Originality/value Our study contributes to career sustainability research by identifying AI awareness as a novel antecedent in socio-technical workplaces. Additionally, we reveal a cross-domain spillover mechanism through which AI awareness undermines employees' career sustainability via work–family conflict. Furthermore, we identify work–family segmentation preference as an individual boundary management strategy that buffers the negative spillover effects of AI awareness.

Future communication networks will need to manage increasingly diverse services, fluctuating traffic demands, and complex operating conditions with minimal manual intervention. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers useful capabilities for predicting network behaviour, identifying faults, and recommending resource-allocation decisions. However, making a prediction is only one part of reliable network management. Operators must also understand why a recommendation was produced, assess its possible consequences, and determine whether it is safe to apply. This paper proposes an explainable, digital-twin-assisted framework for trustworthy AI-native networking, particularly in the context of sixth-generation (6G) communication systems. The framework combines network telemetry, AI-based prediction, digital-twin simulation, explainable recommendations, policy validation, and monitored execution. A virtual representation of the network is used to examine candidate actions before deployment, while the explainability component presents the factors influencing each recommendation. A policy-control layer checks operational restrictions and identifies actions requiring human approval. The proposed design is informed by a focused review of research published during 2024, 2025, and 2026 on AI-enabled digital twins, autonomous network management, generative AI, and AI-native 6G architectures. The review indicates that integrating prediction, simulation, explanation, and feedback offers a promising direction for more transparent network automation. Nevertheless, the framework remains a proposed design and requires implementation and experimental validation. The paper therefore defines research questions, evaluation metrics, and test scenarios for investigating its effectiveness, while discussing the challenges associated with model reliability, digital-twin accuracy, cybersecurity, privacy, and computational overhead..

This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

This conceptual working paper examines how the pursuit of control can be redirected from domination toward democratic cooperation within Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NMR) framework. Its central hypothesis is that reflection can reveal how restricting others’ agency also suppresses knowledge, capabilities and opportunities for shared action. Self-discipline is proposed as a practical link between this insight and the willingness to limit one’s own power. Democratic institutions provide enforceable safeguards where voluntary restraint fails. The analysis connects six equal-ranking basic needs—thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realization and participation, and meaning—with a political assessment of exclusion, discrimination and authoritarian promises of strength. Equal rights are affirmed independently of a person’s productivity or usefulness. What this paper adds: It integrates control, cognitive insight, self-discipline and institutional accountability into a single NMR-based political argument. It distinguishes personal self-restraint from enforceable limits on power and proposes practical measures and questions for empirical investigation. Its role in the series: The paper extends the anthropological and organism-oriented foundations of the NMR framework toward political conduct and democratic institutions, connecting individual self-steering with collective agency and the preservation of shared living conditions. The paper presents a theoretical proposal, not an empirically validated general explanation of prejudice or democratization. It was developed through dialogue with ChatGPT; the nature of this assistance is disclosed in the document.

Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. We recreate the configuration of the OpenAI-provided training example and reproduce the cryptographic verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616) in isolated repository servers, where misconfigured systems enabled token forgery and privilege escalation through basic HTTP requests, Python, and JavaScript. Crucially, the training-example conditions and the Phase One (and later) misconfigurations share the same exploitable patterns. Our analysis explains how Zero Trust Architecture principles neutralize this shared attack vector. Contemporary AI risks derive directly from training and deployment conditions in ambivalent learning environments lacking adequate containment measures.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Environmental decontamination is essential for infection prevention in operating theatres (OTs), yet terminology, evidence and implementation practices vary considerably. Objective: To review the efficacy, safety and implementation of traditional fumigation and contemporary no-touch decontamination technologies. Methods: A structured narrative search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Google Scholar prioritised systematic reviews and OT-specific studies. Formal risk-of-bias and GRADE assessments were not performed. Results: Formaldehyde demonstrates broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity but presents substantial occupational health risks and prolonged environmental persistence. Vaporized hydrogen peroxide and aerosolized hydrogen peroxide are distinct technologies, with vaporized hydrogen peroxide having the strongest evidence base among gaseous approaches, although clinical findings remain variable. Ozone and chlorine dioxide demonstrate antimicrobial efficacy under laboratory conditions, but clinical evidence is limited and stringent safety measures are required. Ultraviolet-C has moderate supporting evidence as an adjunct to manual cleaning. Plasma air treatment and far-UVC require further evaluation, while photocatalytic coatings remain investigational. Clinical trials have not established a clear benefit for plasma air treatment. Conclusion: No single technology suits all OT settings. Selection should consider efficacy, safety, cost and institutional capacity, with manual cleaning remaining fundamental and automated technologies serving as adjuncts. Keywords: Fumigation, Operating Rooms, Communicable Disease Control, Hydrogen Peroxide, Decontamination, Ultraviolet Rays, Review

Recent advances in resting-state functional MRI have enabled non-invasive characterization of large-scale functional networks, providing novel biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring.Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)-particularly resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) and graphtheoretical network analysis-has become the principal noninvasive method for characterizing addiction-related neuroplasticity in humans.This narrative review synthesizes fMRI evidence on addiction-related network reorganization across substance use disorders, including nicotine, alcohol, opioids, cocaine and other stimulants, and cannabis, as well as addiction-adjacent phenomena arising within primary neurological disease, with particular emphasis on impulse control disorders in Parkinson's disease and substance-use vulnerability following traumatic brain injury.The review the rapidly evolving computational layer built on these findings, including graph neural networks, explainable artificial intelligence methods for biomarker attribution, multimodal foundation models pretrained on large unlabeled neuroimaging corpora, and federated learning and harmonization strategies designed to enable multi-site, privacy-preserving biomarker discovery.We also examine fMRI-guided neuromodulation, including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, transcranial direct current stimulation, and deep brain stimulation, as both a mechanistic probe and a treatment strategy, and evaluate the reproducibility, generalizability, and clinical translation barriers that currently constrain this literature.We conclude with a precision-medicine roadmap emphasizing standardized acquisition and analysis pipelines, prospective longitudinal and multimodal designs, externally validated and explainable machine-learning biomarkers, and dedicated connectivity studies in understudied neurological-comorbidity populations.Realizing the clinical potential of fMRI biomarkers of addiction-related neuroplasticity will require moving from descriptive grouplevel neuroimaging findings toward reproducible, individually actionable, and mechanistically interpretable tools.

Accurate nuclei segmentation underpins quantitative computational pathology, yet remains challenging due to morphological variability, weak boundaries, nuclear crowding, and pronounced domain shifts arising from differences in tissue preparation, staining, and acquisition. While deep learning and recent foundation models have improved segmentation performance under matched distributions with the original training data, their generalization across heterogeneous histopathology domains remains limited. We introduce GDBA-Net, a parameter-efficient nuclei segmentation framework built around the proposed Gated Dual-Branch Adapter (GDBA). GDBA-Net adapts a frozen SAM2 encoder by integrating pretrained semantic representations with explicit frequency-derived structural priors. The complementary representations are independently transformed through Grid MLP branches and dynamically integrated using sample-adaptive channel-wise gating, selectively emphasizing structural cues relevant to nuclear delineation. Despite using only 4.3 million trainable parameters, GDBA-Net achieves state-of-the-art in-dataset performance and consistently superior cross-dataset generalization across six diverse nuclei segmentation benchmarks under fully supervised, cross-dataset, and five-shot adaptation protocols, outperforming competing CNN-, transformer-, and foundation model based methods. Comprehensive ablations confirm that these gains arise from the coordinated design of semantic-frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity. By uniting transferable semantic representations with explicit structural priors, GDBA-Net provides a robust, annotation-efficient solution to domain variability in nuclei segmentation. https://github.com/biplabpoudel25/GDBA_Net

Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, and create. It can write text, generate images, assist with programming, and help users turn ideas into useful content. These capabilities offer opportunities in education, healthcare, software development, business, and creative industries. However, the technology also raises important questions about accuracy, privacy, fairness, ownership, and accountability. An AI-generated response may sound convincing while containing incorrect or misleading information. This paper reviews the main applications of generative AI, explains its limitations, and examines the ethical challenges associated with its use. Drawing on research studies and guidance from UNESCO, the World Health Organization (WHO), and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), it argues that successful adoption requires more than powerful models. It also requires careful evaluation, clear rules, and responsible human oversight. This paper is based on a literature review and does not report original experimental results.

documents.abstract: Population ageing and the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence are two defining transformations of the twenty-first century, yet they are rarely considered together. Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) is moving from a technological novelty to an everyday infrastructure. It drafts emails, summarises documents, translates services, produces images, answers health questions and increasingly mediates first-line interactions with organisations. Public debate has focused heavily on schools, universities, workplaces, productivity, misinformation and regulation. Much less attention has been paid to how this transformation intersects with population ageing and the increasingly digital organisation of later life. This omission matters because generative AI is not simply another digital tool. It is becoming part of the infrastructure through which people search for knowledge, assess risks, access services and imagine social groups.Older adults (people aged 65 and older, in line with the statutory retirement age in Switzerland) are not a marginal user group; they are a growing share of the population in many countries and are increasingly expected to navigate digital welfare, health, financial and communication systems. Yet research and design practices often continue to position older adults as late adopters, vulnerable users or recipients of technological solutions rather than as citizens whose agency, knowledge and social representation matter in the future AI ecosystem (Mannheim et al., 2023;Choi et al., 2026).Existing concepts illuminate different aspects of this problem. Research on digital inequality has long conceptualized the "digital divide" as multidimensional, encompassing inequalities in access, skills, use, and outcomes (Dijk, 2020;Bentley et al., 2024). Research on digital inequality has long understood the digital divide as multidimensional. It encompasses inequalities in material access, digital skills, forms and quality of use, and the benefits or disadvantages resulting from use. Research on digital ageism, in turn, examines how age-based assumptions and inequalities are embedded in and reproduced through digital technologies (Mannheim and Köttl, 2024). The two mechanisms underlying the proposed framework, unequal participation and biased representation, are thus already established in the literature, but neither has been specifically applied to generative AI. The doubledivide framework's contribution lies in examining how these mechanisms operate together and may reinforce each other in this context.The proposed double-divide framework distinguishes inequality in engaging with generative AI (Wang et al., 2025) from inequality in being represented by it (Chu et al., 2022): First, older adults may face an AI Participation Divide: inequalities in the ability to access, use, interpret and critically evaluate AI-generated information. Second, they may face an AI Representation Divide: inequalities in how ageing and older adults are represented through AI-generated text, images and decisions. These two divides are distinct but connected. Together, they may shape who benefits from AI and how ageing itself is understood.The promise of generative AI for older adultsGenerative AI can offer substantial benefits in later life. Its natural language interface may lower the barriers that made earlier digital technologies difficult to use. A person who struggles with search engines, online forms or administrative language may ask a chatbot to explain a letter, draft a response, translate information or compare options. Such functions could support autonomy and participation when they are reliable, accessible and embedded in meaningful social contexts. Unlike many earlier digital technologies, generative AI does not require users to navigate complex menus or predefined categories. Its conversational form may allow older adults to start with questions in their own words. In health, AI-driven tools may help explain medical information, support appointment preparation, make complex instructions easier to understand and offer new forms of communication support. For older adults with sensory limitations, low digital confidence or limited formal education, conversational interfaces could be more approachable than menu-based systems. Emerging work on AI-based health technologies and assistive technologies suggests that older adults often see potential benefits, especially when technologies are useful, understandable, trustworthy and aligned with their everyday lives (Enam et al., 2025;Wong et al., 2025). This promise matters. If generative AI is well designed, it could become an important tool for inclusion. The problem is that benefits do not flow automatically from availability. Access to an AI system does not mean that people know what to ask, how to interpret answers or how to judge the accuracy of the output. This is where the first divide begins.In the age of generative AI, the crucial question is not only whether older adults can access generative AI but also whether they have the competence to use it effectively and critically. We define the AI Participation Divide as the unequal capacity to access, use, interpret and evaluate AIgenerated information. Age alone does not determine AI competence. Inequalities within later life reflect accumulated differences in education, income, health, prior occupational exposure to technology, social support and opportunities for digital learning (Enam et al., 2025;Suárez and García-Mariñoso, 2025).The first layer is access and use: Generative AI may be freely available through search engines, smartphones and apps, but this does not mean that its use is evenly distributed. Evidence on AIrelated competencies shows that vulnerable user groups with lower AI knowledge and skills are more likely to be older, less educated and less equipped with privacy-protection skills (Wang et al., 2025).Behavioural evidence on ChatGPT use likewise points to generational and educational differences in adoption (Kacperski et al., 2025). These findings suggest that AI may extend rather than erase established inequalities in digital participation.The second layer is meaningful use: Generative AI requires a new repertoire of practical skills. Users need to know what AI can do, which tasks it is appropriate for, how to formulate prompts, when to provide context and when not to disclose sensitive information. These are not trivial skills. They are learned through experimentation, social support and prior digital confidence. Existing digital experiences can therefore spill over into relationships with AI: People who have felt excluded from digital technology may approach AI with lower confidence, fewer positive experiences and less trust (Bentley et al., 2024).The third layer is interpretation: AI outputs often sound fluent, confident and authoritative, even when they are incomplete, biased or wrong. Older adults, like all users, need to understand that generative AI produces plausible responses rather than verified truth. This distinction is especially important when AI is used for health information, financial questions or legal guidance. The danger is not only non-use but overtrust: a person may use AI and still be disadvantaged because they cannot recognise the limits of the answer.The fourth layer is evaluation. This may become the defining competence of the generative AI era.Evaluation competence includes more than checking whether a statement is factually correct. It also involves recognising when an image, voice, recommendation or personalised message may have been synthetically generated, manipulated or designed to exploit trust. For older adults, this is particularly crucial in domains where trust relationships matter, such as health advice, social communication, banking and public services. Users increasingly need to detect hallucinations, misleading summaries, manipulated images, synthetic voices, scams and AI-generated fake content. Older adults are often framed as vulnerable to online misinformation (Brashier and Schacter, 2020;Li et al., 2025), yet the question should not be reduced to individual deficit. The information environment itself is becoming harder to evaluate, especially for older adults with limited familiarity with generative AI. As services, media and interpersonal communication are increasingly saturated with synthetic content, the critical evaluation of AI becomes a basic condition of social participation. The result is not merely an individual skills gap, but a societal divide in the ability to judge the credibility, authenticity and trustworthiness of AI-mediated information.The AI Participation Divide thus refers to unequal opportunities to access, use, interpret, and evaluate generative AI, and to participate in its design and evaluation. These inequalities do not arise solely from individual abilities, but from the interaction of personal resources with interface design, accessibility, affordability, institutional practices, and available support. Participation is therefore relational, depending on both users and the conditions under which AI is designed, provided, and supported.The second divide concerns representation. The divide lies between the diversity of later life as it is lived and the restricted repertoire through which AI systems often make it visible. Generative AI does not merely help people retrieve information; it also produces text, images and narratives that circulate through society. When people ask AI systems to describe older adults, design services for ageing populations, generate images of later life or summarise what ageing means, the outputs participate in shaping cultural understandings of age. This matters because ageism is already embedded in technology design and AI systems (Martens et al., 2025;Osinga et al., 2026). Reviews of digital technology design show that older adults are frequently framed through assumptions of decline, dependency and lack of competence (Mannheim et al., 2023). Work on sociotechnical ageism shows how AI in care and ageing contexts can reproduce narrow ideas of old age as a problem to be managed through technical solutions (Neves et al., 2023). A scoping review of agerelated bias in AI further shows that age bias may enter AI systems through data, design, modelling and deployment, including through underrepresentation of older adults and biased evaluation of system performance (Chu et al., 2023). Generative AI intensifies this issue because it makes representation scalable. Repetition gives such representations social weight. When similar ageist framings appear across chatbots, image generators, search interfaces and administrative tools, they may come to look less like stereotypes and more like common sense (Martens et al., 2025) Avoiding a double divide requires more than giving older adults access to AI tools. First, AI literacy initiatives must include later life and move beyond basic awareness. These need to teach practical prompting, interpretation of uncertainty, privacy protection and critical evaluation of AI-generated content, including health misinformation, scams, deepfakes and synthetic media. Second, AI systems should be evaluated for age-related bias not only in technical performance but also in the narratives and images they generate. Third, older adults should be involved as co-designers of AI systems and not merely as test users. A recent scoping review shows that older adults are still inconsistently engaged across the design, implementation and evaluation of AI systems (Choi et al., 2026).Participation must include heterogeneous groups of older adults and should address power imbalances in design processes. Fourth, essential health, welfare, financial and public services should retain accessible non-AI alternatives. Age-inclusive AI cannot mean making participation conditional on the ability or willingness to interact with automated systems. Fifth, AI governance should treat age as a core dimension of fairness, inclusion and representation. This includes audit practices that examine whether AI systems exclude older adults from benefits or reproduce ageist assumptions in outputs and decisions. The proposed policy and design recommendations are normative proposals informed by the preceding evidence and conceptual analysis. Their effectiveness should be examined empirically across different populations, settings, and generative AI systems.Age-inclusive AI therefore requires both the capacity to act within AI-mediated environments and the right to be represented by them in ways that reflect the diversity, agency and complexity of later life.Without such efforts, generative AI may widen a double divide in ageing societies, one that limits older adults' capacity to act in AI-mediated environments and narrows how ageing itself is seen.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues

documents.abstract: The rapid development of generative AI is fundamentally transforming creative design disciplines including graphic design, visual communication design, animation, game design, and UI/UX design. Existing studies predominantly address the role of AI within a single discipline, while comparative analyses examining these fields systematically remain limited in the literature. The research conducted by Choudhury, Eisenbart & Kuys (2025) and Song & Abdul Rabu (2025) have clearly revealed the need for discipline-specific comparative studies in sub-fields. The aim of this research is to reveal comparatively in which functions, at which stages, and in what forms of human-AI collaboration AI is utilized within these design disciplines. This systematic review was conducted based on the PRISMA 2020 protocol. A search conducted in the Scopus and Web of Science databases, a total of 100 articles were analyzed, comprising 20 articles representing each of the five visual design disciplines. The results of the analysis reveal that graphic design, artificial intelligence supports concept development and visual production processes, while in visual communication design, it undertakes evaluation and classification functions. In the field of animation, motion generation and character development processes are accelerated, and in game design, it assumes a determining role in procedural content generation and narrative development stages. In UI/UX design, AI contributes to the modeling of user behavior and prototyping processes. The interdisciplinary comparison shows that AI has established itself as a different creative partner in each field, and common challenges such as originality, copyright, and the transformation of designer identity maintain their validity across all disciplines. This research presents an original framework that addresses the use of AI comparatively across five visual design disciplines, emphasizing the necessity of field-based evaluations for design researchers, educators, and practitioners.

The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into Problem-Based Learning (PBL) environments presents new challenges and opportunities for education. The objective of this research is to investigate how AI has been used to promote critical thinking, argumentation, and complex problem-solving within the context of mathematics education or STEM fields. To this end, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted, guided by the PRISMA protocol, analyzing empirical studies published since 2020 and indexed in the Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and ERIC databases. The results indicate that AI transcends the function of a content repository, assuming pedagogical roles such as 'Socratic Coach,' 'Design Partner,' and 'Object of Critical Analysis.' The analysis highlights that the tool's effectiveness depends intrinsically on the quality of prompt engineering and human mediation. Furthermore, AI 'hallucinations' and mathematical inconsistencies do not necessarily need to be perceived as critical flaws; they can emerge as effective pedagogical catalysts for the refinement of logical validation by students. It is concluded that the integration of AI into PBL requires pedagogical intentionality, shifting from prohibitive models to approaches that foster digital literacy and academic integrity within a hybrid intelligence ecosystem.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now widely available to students who learn programming, yet it remains unclear whether higher task performance with AI leads to durable, independent learning. Methods: A narrative review of empirical studies published in 2023–2025 was carried out in September–October 2026. Studies were included if generative AI was used in a learning task and if performance with AI, performance without AI or learning processes were measured. Five controlled or experimental studies formed the core evidence; one qualitative study, one classroom deployment and two surveys were used as supplementary evidence. All bibliographic data were verified against publisher records. Results: AI consistently raised performance while it was available, but its effect on unassisted performance ranged from negative to neutral. Negative effects appeared when learners obtained complete solutions, whereas hint-based or explanation-oriented use reduced or removed them. Several studies suggest that AI may widen the gap between learners with high and low prior knowledge and weaken self-monitoring. Only one study measured delayed retention, and only one measured transfer. Programming courses should therefore assess unassisted performance separately and organise AI use in guided stages.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is increasingly important for adolescents, yet variation in literacy across multiple dimensions and its associations with educational and psychological outcomes remain insufficiently understood. This study identified generative AI literacy profiles among Korean adolescents with generative AI experience ( N = 3,959) using K-means cluster analysis based on information evaluation, communication, creative use, and ethical use. Two profiles were identified: Higher AI Literacy and Lower AI Literacy. The profiles differed primarily in their overall literacy levels rather than in qualitatively distinct patterns across the four dimensions. Adolescents in the Higher AI Literacy profile reported greater generative AI education experience and higher academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being than those in the Lower AI Literacy profile. Differences in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being remained significant after adjustment for gender, school level, academic achievement, and economic status. These findings demonstrate meaningful level-based variation in generative AI literacy among adolescents with generative AI experience and suggest that such variation is associated with educational experience and academic and psychological outcomes. A person-centred perspective may complement variable-centred approaches and inform future research and educational approaches that consider differences in students’ generative AI literacy levels.

Systematic quantitative explanations of the multi-level evolution of emotion regulation remain limited in intelligent music-based intervention research. Traditional music interventions also have limited capacity for dynamic and precise emotion regulation. To address this gap, a generative artificial intelligence (GAI) music therapy framework is developed for multi-level emotion representation and dynamic adaptation. Quantitative transmission pathways are examined across physiological response, psychological perception, and cognitive processing. The framework represents the process from acoustic stimulation input to emotional homeostasis output and compares static fixed-music intervention with GAI-driven dynamic music intervention. The multi-level representation model achieves stable fitting performance, with absolute fitting errors across levels maintained within 0.002-0.005. Under the simulation conditions, the overall transmission efficiency of dynamic music intervention is higher than that of static fixed music intervention. At the 180 s intervention point, the difference in transmission efficiency reaches 0.14, while the difference at the physiological level remains within 0.11-0.14. After 500 training iterations, the steady-state loss decreases to 0.0009. The steady-state fluctuation range of the core parameters is 0.006, the span across parameter groups does not exceed 0.04, and the maximum deviation across repeated parameter fitting is 0.009. The absolute values of all pairwise parameter correlation coefficients remain below 0.12, indicating no apparent multicollinearity in the model solution. Compared with existing studies that mainly examine intervention effects and provide limited quantitative modeling of multi-level coupling, this study develops a serial physiological-psychological-cognitive framework for emotion representation and describes the sequential transmission process through which music stimulation is associated with emotional regulation. The simulation results indicate that dynamic intelligent music stimulation can improve multi-level representation states and may reduce negative emotional responses within the modeled system.
