documents.abstract: Abstract Background Modern forensic DNA methods can recover low-level, trace, and mixed profiles, increasing the importance of contamination control, background DNA, and secondary-transfer-aware interpretation. This cross-sectional online survey of 100 forensic practitioners, contextualised by a targeted narrative literature search, examined perceived human-factor risks, contamination-event experience, and prevention priorities. Responses were analysed descriptively, and each open-ended response was grouped according to its principal recommendation. Results Retained aggregate mean Likert ratings were 4.58 for workload, 4.51 for fatigue, 4.46 for time pressure, 4.42 for improper glove changes, 4.39 for personal protective equipment (PPE) non-compliance, 4.31 for interruptions and distractions, 4.25 for communication failures, and 4.20 for staffing shortages. Sixty-two of 100 respondents reported witnessing or being involved in a DNA contamination incident, and 81 of 100 reported observing a near-miss. Among the 62 respondents reporting contamination-event experience, workload was the most frequently identified primary contributor (29.0%), followed by PPE non-compliance (21.0%), communication failures (16.1%), improper glove changes (12.9%), time pressure (11.3%), laboratory layout or workspace constraints (6.5%), and other factors (3.2%). Open-ended responses ( n = 100) emphasised workload management (44%), training and competency (27%), communication and team coordination (16%), and quality culture and reporting (13%). Conclusions Practitioners perceived DNA contamination as a socio-technical quality issue shaped by interacting operational, behavioural, organisational, and environmental conditions. The author-developed, survey-informed Human-Factor DNA Contamination Framework is presented as a non-scored, non-predictive, and unvalidated conceptual aid for structured risk review and future empirical assessment.
topics: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control

documents.abstract: This study explored how pre-service physics teachers design artificial intelligence (AI)-based pedagogical infrastructure to support metacognitive learning in STEM classrooms. A qualitative interpretive design was employed with 30 pre-service physics teachers enrolled in a physics teacher education program at a university in Kazakhstan. Following two preparatory workshops, participants developed, tested, and refined AI-supported STEM lesson scenarios over 12 weeks. Testing involved peer-based micro-teaching with fellow pre-service teachers acting in simulated student roles; no school students participated. Data comprised individual semi-structured interviews, lesson plans, AI interaction scenarios, prompt sequences, and reflective notes and were examined using reflexive thematic analysis. Six interrelated themes were identified: designing AI-supported STEM lessons; supporting metacognitive regulation and formative assessment; aligning AI use with the physics curriculum and STEM objectives; preserving student agency and ensuring responsible AI use; developing teacher design agency; and addressing conditions for sustainable implementation. Participants' designs generally shifted from using AI to generate ready-made materials toward integrating it more purposefully into structured learning sequences. Pedagogically meaningful scenarios required learners to formulate an initial prediction or solution before consulting AI, verify AI-generated responses using physical laws, calculations, experiments, and reliable sources, and reflect on and revise their reasoning. Reported challenges included inaccurate AI responses, preparation time, unequal access to digital resources, technical difficulties, and variations in the quality of Kazakh- and Russian-language outputs. The findings highlight the importance of preparing pre-service physics teachers for subject-specific, ethically responsible, and pedagogically grounded AI integration. They illustrate design practices intended to scaffold planning, monitoring, scientific verification, evaluation, and reflection. However, the findings concern participants' pedagogical designs and professional perceptions and do not establish improvements in school students' metacognitive regulation or learning outcomes.

In recent years, the emergence of systemic data collection of modern sports has allowed organizations to adopt more data-driven approaches in analyzing sports. Indeed, the wave of popularization of sports analytics, sometimes called statistics in sports, has touched on almost every aspect of the athletic world. Drawing on available data and combining domain knowledge expertise and computational techniques rooted in statistics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, researchers and practitioners of sports analytics can now influence decision-making in sports by analyzing tactical selections, evaluating performance and market values of individual players in team sports, and monitoring the health and fitness of athletes ( Sarlis and Tjortjis, 2020 ; Van Eetvelde et al., 2021 ; Terner and Franks, 2021 ; Bunker and Susnjak, 2022 ; Davis et al., 2022 ; Baumer et al., 2023 ).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Health insurance coverage remains critically low in Sierra Leone, creating barriers to achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and leaving women particularly vulnerable to catastrophic out-of-pocket health expenditures. Understanding which women are most at risk of being uninsured and the specific combination of factors perpetuating their exclusion is essential for designing effective, targeted interventions. This study aimed to develop and evaluate machine learning models to predict health insurance coverage among women in Sierra Leone, identify the most influential sociodemographic and economic predictors, and translate model outputs into actionable, precision-targeted policy recommendations for advancing UHC. Data from the 2019 Sierra Leone Demographic and Health Survey (SLDHS), a nationally representative dataset of 15,574 women, were used. Six classifiers were compared: Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, k-Nearest Neighbours, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost. Cost-sensitive learning strategies were applied to address pronounced class imbalance, where insured women constituted only 3.5% of the sample. To enhance interpretability and support policy translation, Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), were applied to the best-performing interpretable model. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest overall performance, with an AUROC of 0.8857 and a minority class recall of 80.6%. XGBoost performed competitively with an AUROC of 0.869 and was selected for interpretability analysis due to its established compatibility with tree-based explanation workflows. Global SHAP analysis identified region, wealth index, and radio listenership as the three most influential predictors of insurance coverage, with decision-making autonomy variables demonstrating meaningful but secondary contributions. Instance-level waterfall plots and LIME explanations revealed substantial heterogeneity in insurance pathways, distinguishing structurally advantaged, compensatory, and compound-disadvantage profiles among women. Ensemble machine learning models, particularly Gradient Boosting and XGBoost, demonstrate strong predictive utility for identifying uninsured women in low-coverage, resource-limited settings. The integration of SHAP and LIME frameworks bridges the gap between algorithmic performance and actionable policy insight, revealing that insurance coverage is strongly associated with geographic location, economic status, and media exposure. These findings provide an evidence-based framework for precision public health strategies that simultaneously address geographic disparities, economic barriers, and women’s empowerment constraints in Sierra Leone.

ABSTRACT Introduction The evolving role of radiographers in Preliminary Clinical Evaluation (PCE), alongside the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into radiography workflows, is reshaping professional boundaries and enhancing patient care. However, this introduces ethical challenges that may impact PCE performance. This study explored the perspectives of cross‐sectional imaging radiographers on the ethical dimensions of PCE and the potential impact of AI on the future practice of PCE. Method A descriptive qualitative inquiry employing semi‐structured interviews was conducted. A Purposive sampling method was used to recruit twelve cross‐sectional imaging radiographers in a postgraduate medical imaging course at a UK university. Data were analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis with NVivo (v.20.0). Results Participants' clinical experience ranged (2 to 8 years), with 50% ( n = 6) employed in public hospitals and the rest in private or mixed settings. Half ( n = 6) had expertise in both CT/MRI and the rest in CT only. Notably, 42% ( n = 5) practised in multiple countries. Two main themes were developed: (1) Ethical considerations of PCE with subthemes surrounding privacy and confidentiality, communication boundaries, and legal compliance. (2) Prospects of human‐centred PCE in the era of AI, with subthemes including augmentation and support, workflow efficiency, PCE validation and quality assurance. Conclusion Participants shared relevant ethical principles underpinning PCE practice and are cautiously optimistic about the potential impact of AI on PCE. Incorporation of PCE‐specific ethics into radiography education and practice is necessary to ensure consistency, accountability and safety. Cautious integration of AI into radiography practice workflows is recommended to avoid professional deskilling and to preserve expertise.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in advancing inclusive education and preparing educators and institutions for an evolving digital future. As AI technologies shape teaching, learning, and institutional operations, there is a need to align innovation with equity, accessibility, and ethical responsibility. Drawing on theoretical perspectives such as Constructivism, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and Education 5.0, the chapter explores how AI can support individualized learning, enhance participation, and reduce systemic barriers for diverse learners. It further identifies key competencies required for educators and an analysis of institutional readiness. It concludes with policy implications that emphasize inclusive, human-centered, and context-sensitive AI integration.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
